y-m-38-01.title: How many sticker cards are needed? Looking at Hayun's solution
y-m-38-01.thinking.0: Find the first line that goes wrong in the solution
y-m-38-01.s.s1.prompt: Pick the first line that goes wrong in Hayun's solution.
y-m-38-01.s.s2.ok.c1: p and q are natural numbers from 2 to 15.
y-m-38-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make p and q natural numbers from 2 to 15.
y-m-38-01.s.s2.fail.c2: p must be smaller than q.
y-m-38-01.topic: Counting Overlapping Cards in Two Multiple Conditions (Common Multiples and Least Common Multiple)
y-m-38-01.goal: When counting the cases that satisfy at least one of two conditions, judge whether the method of counting overlapping cards is right and find the error, then make your own (p, q) for which that method does not work and say in which cases and how to count.
y-m-38-01.material: Jeongeun's class uses cards numbered from 1. A commemorative sticker is put on cards whose number is a multiple of 4 or a multiple of 6. A card that is both a multiple of 4 and a multiple of 6 also gets only one sticker. Hayun worked out how many stickers are needed in all for cards 1 through 50 as follows.
y-m-38-01.thinking.1: Discover the condition by making examples where the solution's estimate differs from the real count
y-m-38-01.thinking.2: Explain the counterexample and the correct way to count
y-m-38-01.prereq.0: H1 of this set only indicates the level of difficulty of production; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigned it to a particular grade. It assumes you have already learned the basic Number of Cases unit (counting by splitting into cases, counting successive choices, and the permutation and combination symbols nPr, nCr). You know the meanings of multiple, common multiple and least common multiple.
y-m-38-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write out the multiples of 4 and the multiples of 6 from 1 to 50 yourself.
y-m-38-01.s.s1.hint.1: Find the numbers that are in both lists and compare them with the numbers the solution said overlap.
y-m-38-01.s.s1.line.0: The multiples of 4 are 4, 8, …, 48, which is 12 cards.
y-m-38-01.s.s1.line.1: The multiples of 6 are 6, 12, …, 48, which is 8 cards.
y-m-38-01.s.s1.line.2: The cards that are on both lists are common multiples of 4 and 6, and common multiples are multiples of 4×6=24, so there are two: card 24 and card 48.
y-m-38-01.s.s1.line.3: The 2 overlapping cards must be counted only once, so 12+8−2=18 cards are needed.
y-m-38-01.s.s1.explain: Line 3 went wrong. Card 12 is a multiple of 4 and of 6, but it is not a multiple of 24. The common multiples of 4 and 6 are the multiples of their least common multiple 12 (12, 24, 36, 48), so four cards overlap, and the real number of sticker cards is 12+8−4=16 (listing cards 1 to 50 directly also gives 16). The counts in lines 1 and 2 are correct, and line 4 is a calculation that uses the overlap count from line 3.
y-m-38-01.s.s2.prompt: This time, stickers are put on the cards numbered 1 to 60 whose number is a multiple of p or a multiple of q. (p and q are natural numbers from 2 to 15, and p<q.) If you count like Hayun, saying "the cards that fit both rules are the cards that are multiples of p×q," the count differs from the real number of overlapping cards. Make two different pairs (p, q) for which this happens.
y-m-38-01.s.s2.hint.0: Let p=4, q=6. List directly the numbers from 1 to 60 that fit both rules, then compare them with the multiples of p×q.
y-m-38-01.s.s2.hint.1: Change p and q and make the same comparison each time. Then organize in a table what differs between p and q when the two values are the same and when they are different.
y-m-38-01.s.s2.ok.c3: The real number of overlapping cards and the number of cards that are multiples of p×q are different.
y-m-38-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The real number of overlapping cards and the number of cards that are multiples of p×q are the same. List directly the numbers within 60 that fit both rules and compare.
y-m-38-01.s.s2.explain: For (4, 6), the common multiples within 60 are 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, which is 5 cards, but the multiples of 24 are only 24 and 48, two cards. For (10, 12), there is one common multiple, 60, but there is no multiple of 120. If p and q have a common divisor greater than 1, the least common multiple is smaller than p×q, so counting only multiples of the product misses overlapping cards. For the coprime pair (3, 5), the least common multiple equals the product, so the estimate is right. Also, for (12, 14), even though they have a common divisor, the least common multiple 84 is greater than 60, so both values are 0 cards and equal.
y-m-38-01.s.s3.prompt: Write a short note to Hayun. Using the (p, q) you just made, or the case of 4 and 6, as an example, write with numbers what to be careful about when counting the cards that fit both rules.
y-m-38-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write down the first few numbers that are on both the list of multiples of 4 and the list of multiples of 6.
y-m-38-01.s.s3.hint.1: For the (p, q) you just made, write the numbers that really overlap and the multiples of p×q side by side and compare them.
y-m-38-01.s.s3.placeholder: e.g., Hayun, the common multiples of 4 and 6 are ..., so ...
y-m-38-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you use numbers to say how the overlapping cards should be found?
y-m-38-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say when the method of counting only multiples of the product is wrong (when there is a common divisor)?
y-m-38-01.s.s3.model.0: The common multiples of 4 and 6 are not the multiples of 4×6=24 but the multiples of the least common multiple 12. Four cards overlap, 12, 24, 36, 48, so 12+8−4=16 cards is right. If you say only the two cards 24 and 48 overlap, you get 18 cards, which is wrong.
y-m-38-01.s.s3.model.1: For my (10, 12), the product is 120, so there is no multiple of 120 within 60, but in fact card 60 is counted twice. The overlapping cards must be counted as multiples of the least common multiple 60, not of the product. For 4 and 6, too, you must subtract the 4 multiples of 12 to get 16 cards.
y-m-38-01.s.s3.model.2: Count with the least common multiple 12, not the product 24. There are 4 multiples of 12, so 12+8-4=16 cards.

y-m-38-02.title: The number of ways to make a round trip: why Hyunseo's and Hajun's answers differ
y-m-38-02.topic: The number of round-trip routes that changes with conditions
y-m-38-02.goal: Know that a condition not written in the problem (may you use the same road again on the way back?) changes the answer, point out the information needed, and find on your own several cases that give a given value in a new situation where the conditions are fixed.
y-m-38-02.material: There are 4 different roads between village A and village B. Hyunseo said, "The number of ways to go from A to B and come back to A is 4×4=16 in all," and Hajun said, "No, it's 4×3=12." The problem says only, "How many ways are there to go from A to B and come back?" Count the road going and the road coming back as different, in order.
y-m-38-02.thinking.0: Judge whether the information is enough
y-m-38-02.thinking.1: Find the condition that changes the answer
y-m-38-02.thinking.2: Find several solutions under a constraint
y-m-38-02.prereq.0: H1 of this set is only a production difficulty level; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigned it to a particular grade. Assume the basic counting unit (counting by splitting into cases, counting choices made one after another, the symbols nPr and nCr for permutations and combinations) has already been learned. You know how to count the cases when choosing roads happens one after another.
y-m-38-02.s.s1.prompt: If you judge using only the information written in the problem, which statement fits best?
y-m-38-02.s.s1.hint.0: Write down how many roads each of Hyunseo and Hajun thought the road back is chosen from.
y-m-38-02.s.s1.hint.1: Name the roads 가, 나, 다, 라, and when "going by 가," list the roads for coming back yourself.
y-m-38-02.s.s1.o.a: Hyunseo's 16 is likely right. This is because the road back can also be chosen from 4.
y-m-38-02.s.s1.r.a: You read it as allowing the road passed on the way there to be used again on the way back. That reading is natural, but the problem does not say so.
y-m-38-02.s.s1.o.b: Hajun's 12 is right. A road already passed cannot be used as the road back, so 16 counts too many.
y-m-38-02.s.s1.r.b: You read it as not using the road passed on the way there when coming back. The problem does not state such a limit.
y-m-38-02.s.s1.o.c: The problem alone cannot decide between the two. The rule for the road back is not written.
y-m-38-02.s.s1.r.c: This judgment recognized that the two answers came from different assumptions.
y-m-38-02.s.s1.o.d: The answer is 8. You must count the 4 roads going and the 4 roads coming back separately and add them.
y-m-38-02.s.s1.r.d: You added choosing the road going and then choosing the road back as if they were separate events rather than events linked one after the other.
y-m-38-02.s.s1.explain: 16 is the value from reading it as allowing the same road on the way back, and 12 is the value from reading it as not using on the way back the road used going. This condition is not written in the problem, so you must state your assumption or ask.
y-m-38-02.s.s1.acc.0: When no limit is written, it is also natural to read it as allowed to use again. But you must state that you read it that way.
y-m-38-02.s.s2.prompt: To fix the answer to one, what question must you ask the teacher?
y-m-38-02.s.s2.hint.0: Compare which numbers differ in the expressions that make 16 and 12.
y-m-38-02.s.s2.hint.1: Write in one sentence the condition that makes that number differ.
y-m-38-02.s.s2.o.a: When coming back, may we pass again the road we passed going?
y-m-38-02.s.s2.r.a: This is a question that points exactly to the condition that separates the two answers.
y-m-38-02.s.s2.o.b: Which of the four roads gets there the fastest?
y-m-38-02.s.s2.r.b: Even if you know the fast road, the number of roads stays the same. Sort out the information that changes the count from the information that does not.
y-m-38-02.s.s2.o.c: How many kilometers is it between A and B?
y-m-38-02.s.s2.r.c: Distance has nothing to do with the number of ways.
y-m-38-02.s.s2.o.d: Are the names of all four roads different from each other?
y-m-38-02.s.s2.r.d: It has already been fixed that there are 4 different roads.
y-m-38-02.s.s2.explain: What splits the count is "may the road used going be used again coming back." If allowed, 4×4=16; if not allowed, 4×3=12.
y-m-38-02.s.s3.prompt: This time the rules are fixed. There are n roads between A and B, and m roads between B and C. You go from A through B to C and come back from C through B to A. ① The road going and the road coming back are counted as different, and ② on the way back, you cannot use again in the same section a road passed going. Find two different pairs (n, m) for which the number of ways to make this round trip is exactly 144. (Count a pair with n and m swapped as the same example.)
y-m-38-02.s.s3.hint.0: For n=2, 3, 4, first write in terms of n the number that combines the cases chosen going and chosen coming back.
y-m-38-02.s.s3.hint.1: Once you fix n, check what value the expression in m must have, and try m in order starting from 2.
y-m-38-02.s.s3.var.n: Number of roads between A and B, n
y-m-38-02.s.s3.var.m: Number of roads between B and C, m
y-m-38-02.s.s3.ok.c1: n and m are natural numbers from 2 to 12.
y-m-38-02.s.s3.fail.c1: Please make n and m natural numbers from 2 to 12.
y-m-38-02.s.s3.ok.c2: The number of ways to make the round trip is exactly 144.
y-m-38-02.s.s3.fail.c2: With this (n, m) it is not 144. Work out, for each section, the number of roads chosen going and the number of roads you can choose coming back.
y-m-38-02.s.s3.explain: Going gives n×m ways; coming back, since the road used going in the same section is removed, gives (m−1)×(n−1) ways in sequence, so the total is n(n−1)×m(m−1) ways. The only cases where this value is 144 are (2, 9), (9, 2), and (4, 4). This is because 144=2×72=12×12 splits that way.

y-m-38-03.title: When two people stand right next to each other or stand apart, which has more cases?
y-m-38-03.topic: Comparing the cases where two people are neighbors and not neighbors in a line-up
y-m-38-03.goal: Revise your judgment by adding more examples, seeing how the more-or-less of "two people are neighbors" and "not neighbors" changes as the number of people changes, and explain the number of non-neighbor cases in different ways.
y-m-38-03.material: n people stand in a line to take a photo. Different standing orders count as different cases. Among them, pay attention to two people, Jisu and Minho. The case where the two stand right next to each other is called "neighbor," and the case where one or more other people stand between them is called "apart." The question is, "Which has more cases, neighbor or apart?"
y-m-38-03.thinking.0: Revise your expectation after seeing the result
y-m-38-03.thinking.1: Work out whether you can generalize from a few examples
y-m-38-03.thinking.2: Explain the same value in different ways
y-m-38-03.prereq.0: H1 of this set is only a production difficulty level; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigned it to a particular grade. Assume the basic counting unit (counting by splitting into cases, counting choices made one after another, the symbols nPr and nCr for permutations and combinations) has already been learned. You know the number of ways n! to line up n different people in a row.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.prompt: As the number of people changes, predict at each step which of neighbor and apart has more, and after seeing new information, decide whether to revise or keep your judgment.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.hint.0: After writing your expectation from the result for 3 people, compare in one line whether that expectation is right each time new information appears.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.hint.1: Write the number of neighbor cases and the total in terms of the number of people n, and test whether you can see a pattern.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.0.info: There are 6 ways in all for 3 people (Jisu, Minho, Sua) to stand. Written in the order Jisu, Minho, Sua, (Jisu Minho Sua), (Minho Jisu Sua), (Sua Jisu Minho), (Sua Minho Jisu) are neighbors, and (Jisu Sua Minho), (Minho Sua Jisu) are apart. Neighbors are 4 ways and apart is 2 ways.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: Even if the number of people grows to 5 or 10, will neighbors keep being more? Choose the best expectation with the information you have now.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.0.after: From the result for 3 people alone, expectations can split. It is true that neighbors look more numerous, but how it changes as the number of people grows must be checked directly.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Even if the number of people grows, the neighbor cases will keep being more.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You extended the tendency of the single example of 3 people as it is. It is a possible expectation, but there is only one basis.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: If the number of people grows, there are more places to stand apart, so apart will become more.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You changed direction in your expectation based on the number of places growing. But you have not yet checked any example.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: There is only one example, 3 people, so I do not know yet. I have to work out 4 people and 5 people.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This judgment knows the basis is lacking and tries to check more.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Neighbor and apart are always the same, whatever the number of people.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This does not match the result for 3 people we just saw (4 ways and 2 ways).
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.1.info: There are 24 ways in all for 4 people (Jisu, Minho, Sua, Hajun) to stand. Of these, neighbors are 12 ways and apart is also 12 ways.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: You looked at the results for 3 and 4 people together. What about 5 or more people?
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.1.after: With 4 people the two numbers of cases became equal. The tendency of 3 people, where neighbors were ahead, did not simply continue. You can know which side will be ahead only by checking 5 or more people.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Going from 3 to 4 people, the difference between neighbor and apart shrank. If it grows more, apart may get ahead of neighbor.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You predicted a direction by looking at how the two results changed.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: The state where neighbor is more than or equal to apart will continue.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: It does not contradict the two results so far, but it does not reflect the trend of the difference shrinking.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Neighbor and apart are always the same.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: With 3 people they were different, 4 ways and 2 ways.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Being equal for 4 people may be a coincidence. I will count 5 people myself to check.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is a careful judgment that does not conclude from just two results.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.2.info: There are 120 ways in all for 5 people to stand. If you treat Jisu and Minho as one block, there are 24 ways to line up 4 blocks, and the order of the two people inside the block has 2 ways, so neighbors are 48 ways and apart is 72 ways.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: You have seen the results for 3, 4, and 5 people. What happens when there are many, like 10 or 20 people?
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.2.after: With 5 people, apart became more than neighbor for the first time. The ratio of neighbors keeps shrinking. Shall we check directly with 10 people?
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Apart will keep being more, and the difference from neighbor will grow wider.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You extended the flow of the three results (neighbor ahead → equal → apart ahead) in your expectation.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Apart will be more, but the ratio to neighbor will hardly change.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: The ratio that neighbors take of the whole is shrinking: 4/6 for 3 people, 12/24 for 4 people, 48/120 for 5 people.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: There will be some numbers of people where neighbor becomes more again.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The three results show no such flow. It is an expectation that turns back without a basis.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: It is hard to speak about 10 or 20 people from only three results. I will calculate directly to check.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This is a judgment that is careful about generalizing from three examples.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.3.info: There are 3,628,800 ways for 10 people to stand. Neighbors are 2×9!=725,760 ways and apart is 2,903,040 ways, so apart is exactly 4 times neighbor.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.3.ask: To say "if n is 5 or more, apart is always more than neighbor," what basis fits best?
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.3.after: Adding more examples increases belief, but "all n" is settled when it can be shown with an expression that does not depend on n. Neighbors are 2/n of the whole, so for n=4 it is exactly half, and for n of 5 or more it is less than half.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.3.o.a: I checked both cases, 5 people and 10 people, so it is enough evidence. There is no need to check more.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.3.r.a: Two examples cannot speak for all n. Examples only add to the evidence.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.3.o.b: Neighbors are 2/n of the whole (2×(n−1)!÷n!). If n is 5 or more, 2/n is less than 1/2.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.3.r.b: This judgment built its evidence with an expression that holds regardless of n.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.3.o.c: If the number of people grows, all cases get more, so apart is bound to get more than neighbor too.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.3.r.c: "All cases get more" is true of neighbor too, so it does not serve as a basis for comparing the two cases.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.3.o.d: If I calculate directly for n=20, 30, 50 too and get the same result, I conclude it always holds.
y-m-38-03.s.s1.st.3.r.d: It is good extra evidence, but there are still n that you did not calculate, so it does not guarantee "always."
y-m-38-03.s.s1.reflect: With 3 people neighbor was ahead, with 4 people they were equal, and from 5 people apart was ahead. Whether you kept your first expectation or changed it, the key point is that a few examples make it hard to say "always," and you can settle it when there is an expression that does not depend on n.
y-m-38-03.s.s2.prompt: Of the 120 ways for 5 people to stand, the cases where Jisu and Minho are apart are 72 ways. Pick one method and explain with numbers why 72 comes out.
y-m-38-03.s.s2.hint.0: Decide whether you can find the number of neighbor cases first, or whether it is easier to first make the non-adjacent places.
y-m-38-03.s.s2.hint.1: Write separately the ways the other 3 people stand and the places the two people go.
y-m-38-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: At each step of the method you chose, did numbers (24, 48, 6, 12, and so on) appear, and did you say where those numbers came from?
y-m-38-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you remember the order of Jisu and Minho (2 ways)?
y-m-38-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you check whether you also get 72 with another method?
y-m-38-03.s.s2.model.0: First count the cases where Jisu and Minho are neighbors. If you treat the two people as one block, there are 24 ways to line up 4 blocks, and the order of the two people inside the block has 2 ways, so it is 48 ways. Subtracting this 48 from the total 120 gives 72 ways.
y-m-38-03.s.s2.model.1: First line up the other 3 people, which is 6 ways. Put Jisu and Minho into two different places among the 4 places, between the 3 people and at the two ends, which is 4×3=12 ways. Done this way, the two people do not stick together, so it is 6×12=72 ways.

y-m-38-04.title: Ways to split 9 people into three teams of 3: why Seoyeon's and Dohyeon's answers differ
y-m-38-04.topic: Splitting into teams of the same size: when teams are distinguished and when they are not
y-m-38-04.goal: Know that "the number of ways to split" has a different value depending on whether the teams are distinguished, explain how many times the same split is counted when they are not distinguished, and judge whether the same thing happens when all the team sizes are different.
y-m-38-04.material: We want to split 9 club students (all different people) into three teams of 3. Seoyeon said, "C(9,3)×C(6,3)×C(3,3)=84×20×1=1680 ways," and Dohyeon said, "It's 1680 divided by 6, which is 280 ways." (C(9,3) is the number of ways to choose 3 of 9 people.)
y-m-38-04.thinking.0: Find a condition that is not in the problem
y-m-38-04.thinking.1: Find the line with the error in the solution
y-m-38-04.thinking.2: Explain why the same case is counted several times
y-m-38-04.prereq.0: H1 of this set is only a production difficulty level; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigned it to a particular grade. Assume the basic counting unit (counting by splitting into cases, counting choices made one after another, the symbols nPr and nCr for permutations and combinations) has already been learned. You know that the combination C(n, r) is the number of ways to choose r of n without regard to order.
y-m-38-04.s.s1.prompt: What is the most fitting judgment about Seoyeon's and Dohyeon's answers?
y-m-38-04.s.s1.hint.0: In the small example of splitting 6 people into three teams of 2 (가, 나, 다), write out one split yourself.
y-m-38-04.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many ways you can write the same split by changing only the order in which you give the teams names.
y-m-38-04.s.s1.o.a: Seoyeon's 1680 is right. Dohyeon's division by 6 is an unnecessary calculation.
y-m-38-04.s.s1.r.a: You missed that Seoyeon's expression is a value that also distinguishes the order in which the teams are chosen first.
y-m-38-04.s.s1.o.b: Dohyeon's 280 is right. The same three teams must be counted as one even if the counting order differs, so 1680 is too many.
y-m-38-04.s.s1.r.b: You read it from the start as not distinguishing the teams. You need to check whether the problem says so.
y-m-38-04.s.s1.o.c: Both are wrong. The answer is 84, the number of ways to choose one team.
y-m-38-04.s.s1.r.c: 84 is the value of fixing only one team. You did not count the task of fixing the other teams.
y-m-38-04.s.s1.o.d: Depending on whether the teams are distinguished from each other, both values can be the answer.
y-m-38-04.s.s1.r.d: This judgment pointed out that the two answers came from different readings.
y-m-38-04.s.s1.explain: Seoyeon's expression counts the ways of choosing the first team, the second team, and the third team in order, so it is the value that distinguishes the teams (1680). If the teams have no names, the cases that differ only in the order the same three teams were chosen merge into one, giving 280. The problem does not have this condition, so which of the two is the answer depends on the condition.
y-m-38-04.s.s1.acc.0: It is natural to read "split into three teams" with no marking as teams that are not distinguished. But you must state that assumption.
y-m-38-04.s.s1.acc.1: If the teams have names like Team 1, Team 2, Team 3, the answer is 1680. But the problem has no such words, so you must state your assumption.
y-m-38-04.s.s2.prompt: Suppose we split six people into three teams of 2 and do not distinguish the teams. Pick the line where Jiho's solution goes wrong.
y-m-38-04.s.s2.hint.0: Reread the definition to see whether C(6,2)=15 is "the number of ways to choose 2 people" or "the number of ways to line up 2 people."
y-m-38-04.s.s2.hint.1: With 6 people A, B, C, D, E, F, write out yourself how many times the one split {A,B}, {C,D}, {E,F} appears among the 90.
y-m-38-04.s.s2.line.0: If you count C(6,2)=15 first, then C(4,2)=6, then C(2,2)=1 in sequence, it is 15×6×1=90 ways when the teams are given names.
y-m-38-04.s.s2.line.1: The order of lining up the 2 people inside each team has 2 ways each, so we must divide by 2×2×2=8.
y-m-38-04.s.s2.line.3: But the number of ways must be a natural number, so we must check the calculation again.
y-m-38-04.s.s2.explain: Line 2 goes wrong. The combination C counts without distinguishing the order of the people already chosen, so there is no need to divide by the order inside the team. When the teams have no names, what you must divide by is 3!=6, the number of cases where only the order of choosing the same three teams changes. Then 90÷6=15 ways, and listing the 6 people directly also gives 15 ways. Line 4 is correct as a check that noticed the value in line 3 is not a natural number.
y-m-38-04.s.s3.prompt: This time, suppose we split 9 people into three teams of 2, 3, and 4 (the teams have no names). In this case, since we do not distinguish the teams, should we divide by 3!?
y-m-38-04.s.s3.hint.0: Write the one split {가나}, {다라마}, {바사아자} changing only the order of the teams. Do they become different splits?
y-m-38-04.s.s3.hint.1: Write the sizes of the three teams side by side and check whether there are teams of the same size.
y-m-38-04.s.s3.o.a: We should divide. The teams have no names, so the same split is counted 6 times.
y-m-38-04.s.s3.r.a: You carried over the rule for the case where all team sizes are the same.
y-m-38-04.s.s3.o.b: We do not divide. The team sizes are different, so they are already distinguished from each other.
y-m-38-04.s.s3.r.b: You recognized that the size of the team already distinguishes the teams.
y-m-38-04.s.s3.o.c: Divide by 2!. Only swapping two teams gives the same split.
y-m-38-04.s.s3.r.c: You did not look at which two teams have the same size. The sizes of the three teams are all different.
y-m-38-04.s.s3.o.d: Whether to divide depends on whether the teams have names, so we cannot know.
y-m-38-04.s.s3.r.d: In this case, even without team names, the teams are distinguished by their sizes.
y-m-38-04.s.s3.explain: The teams of 2, 3, and 4 are already distinguished by size. Choosing the first team of 2 people as C(9,2)=36 and the second team of 3 people as C(7,3)=35, the rest is the team of 4, so it is 36×35=1260 ways and there is no need to divide separately.
y-m-38-04.s.s4.prompt: Explain why, when splitting 9 people into three teams of 3 and the teams have no names, it is 280 ways. Write it by working out how many times one split like {가,나,다}, {라,마,바}, {사,아,자} is counted in Seoyeon's expression.
y-m-38-04.s.s4.hint.0: Write all the ways to give the names Team 1, Team 2, Team 3 to the three teams of one split.
y-m-38-04.s.s4.hint.1: Compare how those ways should be counted when there are no names.
y-m-38-04.s.s4.placeholder: Example: This split is counted ... times in Seoyeon's expression, and ...
y-m-38-04.s.s4.selfAssess.0: Did I connect the reason I wrote that one split is counted 6 times with the number of ways to name the teams (3!)?
y-m-38-04.s.s4.selfAssess.1: Did I state that when the teams have names, these 6 are counted as different cases?
y-m-38-04.s.s4.selfAssess.2: Did I say why the calculation 1680÷6=280 is needed?
y-m-38-04.s.s4.model.0: Even the one split {가,나,다}, {라,마,바}, {사,아,자} has 3!=6 ways to give the teams the names Team 1, Team 2, Team 3, so if there are names it is counted 6 times. If there are no names, these 6 are all the same split. So 1680÷6=280.
y-m-38-04.s.s4.model.1: Seoyeon's 1680 is a value counted while also distinguishing the order of the first team chosen, the second team, and the third team. The 6 ways (3!) that only change the order of choosing the same three teams are included as different cases. If you do not distinguish the teams, those 6 are one, so dividing by 6 gives 280.

y-m-38-05.title: The number of three-digit even numbers: do three methods reach the same value?
y-m-38-05.topic: Counting three-digit even numbers made of different digits (the condition on 0 and splitting into cases)
y-m-38-05.goal: Under the conditions that 0 cannot come first and the ones digit must be even, find the errors that come from the order of counting, compare different ways of counting, and say what grounds let you trust the result and what worries remain.
y-m-38-05.material: From 10 cards with 0, 1, 2, …, 9 written on them one each, choose 3 different cards and place them in a row to make a three-digit number. The 0 card cannot be placed at the front (the hundreds place). If the card in the ones place is one of 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, the number is even. How many three-digit even numbers can be made in all? Harin decided the ones place first and solved it as below.
y-m-38-05.thinking.0: Find the error in a solution
y-m-38-05.thinking.2: Say what grounds there are to trust the result and what worries remain
y-m-38-05.prereq.0: H1 of this set is only a production difficulty level; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigned it to a particular grade. Assume the basic counting unit (counting by splitting into cases, counting choices made one after another, the symbols nPr and nCr for permutations and combinations) has already been learned. You have counted the number of ways to choose in order from different things.
y-m-38-05.s.s1.prompt: Pick the wrong line in Harin's solution.
y-m-38-05.s.s1.hint.0: List the cards that can come in the hundreds place when the ones card is 0 and when it is 2.
y-m-38-05.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the number of choices for the hundreds place in the two cases, and look at which case the statement in line 2 applies to.
y-m-38-05.s.s1.line.0: One of 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 comes in the ones place, so there are 5 ways.
y-m-38-05.s.s1.line.1: The hundreds place is chosen from 1 to 9, which are not 0, so there are 9 ways in any case.
y-m-38-05.s.s1.line.2: The tens place is chosen from the 8 cards left after removing the two cards already used, so there are 8 ways.
y-m-38-05.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is wrong. If the ones place is 0, the hundreds place has 9 ways, 1 to 9, but if the ones place is 2, 4, 6, 8, you cannot use that card, so the hundreds place has 8 ways. It is not "9 ways in any case." So Harin's 5×9×8=360 counted one extra way for the hundreds place when the ones place is 2, 4, 6, 8. Lines 1 and 3 are correct, and line 4 multiplied the wrong value.
y-m-38-05.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the methods that can correctly count the number of three-digit even numbers. (Before finding the calculation result, judge only whether the method is correct.)
y-m-38-05.s.s2.hint.0: For each method, check "does this method count every case, with none missed and each only once?"
y-m-38-05.s.s2.hint.1: Apply methods a and c to the case where there are only three cards, 0, 1, 2, and compare with the count you list directly.
y-m-38-05.s.s2.o.a: From 5×9×8=360, subtract one for the case of using 0 to fix it to 359.
y-m-38-05.s.s2.r.a: You subtracted an arbitrary number without working out which case was miscounted and by how much.
y-m-38-05.s.s2.o.b: Split into the case where the ones place is 0 and the case where it is not, count each, and add them.
y-m-38-05.s.s2.r.b: This is a method that splits into cases at the point where the number of choices for the hundreds place changes.
y-m-38-05.s.s2.o.c: Remove 0 from the ones place and count 4×9×8 to eliminate the cases where 0 comes first.
y-m-38-05.s.s2.r.c: The 0 in the ones place is a case with no problem. You mixed it up with the problem of 0 coming first.
y-m-38-05.s.s2.o.d: Count all three-digit numbers made of different digits, then exclude the cases where the ones place is odd.
y-m-38-05.s.s2.r.d: This is a method that counts the side that is easy to count exactly and gets the rest from it.
y-m-38-05.s.s2.o.e: Split into the case where the hundreds place is even and the case where it is odd, count each, and add them.
y-m-38-05.s.s2.r.e: This is a method that, even with a changed counting order, splits into cases at the point where the number of ways changes.
y-m-38-05.s.s2.explain: For b, if the ones place is 0 it is 9×8=72, otherwise 4×8×8=256, so adding gives 328. For d, subtract from the 9×9×8=648 three-digit numbers made of different digits the 5×8×8=320 with an odd ones place to get 328. For e, if the hundreds place is even it is 4×4×8=128, and if odd 5×5×8=200, so 328. For a, you have to count exactly the cases where the hundreds place and ones place become the same from 360, not 359, and for c, you remove even the 0 in the ones place and so actually miss some.
y-m-38-05.s.s3.prompt: Counting with the three methods b, d, e gave 328 each time. Can you trust this value? Write the grounds for trusting it together with the worries that still remain (or ways to check more).
y-m-38-05.s.s3.hint.0: Compare, one line each, how each of the three methods handled which condition.
y-m-38-05.s.s3.hint.1: Find what condition all three methods believe in equally, and imagine what would happen if that condition were wrong.
y-m-38-05.s.s3.placeholder: Example: I counted with different methods and ... but ...
y-m-38-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I say why the fact that different methods gave the same value raises trust?
y-m-38-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I name as a worry that the three methods share the same assumption (for example, 0 cannot come first)?
y-m-38-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I suggest a concrete way to check, such as listing a small case directly and comparing?
y-m-38-05.s.s3.model.0: The three methods counted in different orders and all got 328, so it is believable. But if all three methods thought about "0 cannot come first" in the same way, they could make the same mistake together. So I will reduce the cards to the three cards 0, 1, 2, list directly (102, 120, 210, which is 3), and check whether the value counted by the methods is also 3.
y-m-38-05.s.s3.model.1: Counting in several ways and all agreeing on 328 raised my confidence. But if an assumption that all the methods use in common (for example, the ones place must be even) is wrong, the three values could be wrong together. Listing a small case directly and seeing whether it matches the value from the methods is a way to check.

y-m-38-06.title: Is "choose more and the number of ways also grows" always right?
y-m-38-06.topic: How the number of combinations changes with the number chosen, and a counterexample
y-m-38-06.goal: Know that the fact that a few values grew in a row does not let you say "it always grows," find in the table yourself an r where the value does not grow and use it as a counterexample, and predict where the value is largest for a different n and explain why.
y-m-38-06.material: There are 9 different kinds of fruit. Choose r kinds of them (the order of choosing is not distinguished) to make a gift box. The number of kinds of box is C(9,r), the number of ways to choose r kinds. Minseo saw that for r=0, 1, 2, 3 the values keep growing, 1, 9, 36, 84, and said, "If you choose one more fruit, the number of kinds of box you can make always grows too."
y-m-38-06.thinking.0: Judge whether the evidence is enough to generalize
y-m-38-06.thinking.1: Make a counterexample from the table
y-m-38-06.prereq.0: H1 of this set is only a production difficulty level; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigned it to a particular grade. Assume the basic counting unit (counting by splitting into cases, counting choices made one after another, the symbols nPr and nCr for permutations and combinations) has already been learned. You know the meaning of the number of combinations C(n, r).
y-m-38-06.s.s1.prompt: What is the most fitting judgment about Minseo's statement from the information seen so far?
y-m-38-06.s.s1.hint.0: Write side by side the range of r that Minseo checked and the range of possible r (0 to 9) and compare them.
y-m-38-06.s.s1.hint.1: Pick one of the values of r not yet checked and calculate C(9,r) yourself.
y-m-38-06.s.s1.o.a: It grew four times in a row, from r=0 to 3, so we can take it as growing for all r.
y-m-38-06.s.s1.r.a: You believed it was a rule because there were four examples. You still do not know what happens at the r you have not seen.
y-m-38-06.s.s1.o.b: r=0 is the case of choosing nothing, so this evidence cannot be used at all.
y-m-38-06.s.s1.r.b: It is true that r=0 is a special case, but you threw out even the other examples because of that one.
y-m-38-06.s.s1.o.c: Growing four times is evidence, but it can break at an r we have not seen.
y-m-38-06.s.s1.r.c: This judgment accepts the examples seen so far as evidence while pointing out that there is a range not yet tested.
y-m-38-06.s.s1.o.d: If the number chosen changes, the numbers of ways are not related to each other, so comparing them is meaningless in itself.
y-m-38-06.s.s1.r.d: You can compare the numbers of ways even if the numbers chosen differ. There is also no basis to conclude they are not related.
y-m-38-06.s.s1.explain: The four examples support the claim, but "always" is a statement about all r. It could differ at r we have not seen (4 or more), so we need to test more.
y-m-38-06.s.s2.prompt: The values of C(9,r) for r=0 to 9 in order are 1, 9, 36, 84, 126, 126, 84, 36, 9, 1. Find three different r where Minseo's statement breaks, that is, where C(9,r) does not become larger than C(9,r−1) (is equal or smaller).
y-m-38-06.s.s2.hint.0: In the table, pair up two neighboring values and check one at a time whether the later value is larger than the earlier one.
y-m-38-06.s.s2.hint.1: Find the first pair where the later value is not larger than the earlier one, and look at whether everything after it is the same.
y-m-38-06.s.s2.ok.c1: r is a natural number from 1 to 9.
y-m-38-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make r a natural number from 1 to 9. (You compare with r−1, so you cannot use 0.)
y-m-38-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The number of ways to choose r kinds did not grow compared with choosing r−1 kinds.
y-m-38-06.s.s2.fail.c2: At this r the value grew. In the table, look for where the value stops getting larger.
y-m-38-06.s.s2.explain: At r=5 it is 126, the same as r=4 (does not grow), and at r=6, 7, 8, 9 it decreases to 84, 36, 9, 1. So r=5, 6, 7, 8, 9 are all counterexamples that break Minseo's statement. r=5 is the case where it does not grow because it is "equal," and the rest are cases where it "decreases."
y-m-38-06.s.s3.prompt: With 9 kinds of fruit, the values at r=4 and r=5 were equal at 126. With 10 kinds of fruit, at which r is the value largest? Write your prediction and the reason. (Choosing r kinds can also be seen as the number of ways to leave some unchosen.)
y-m-38-06.s.s3.hint.0: Check with a small example (choosing 1 of 4) whether each way of choosing r determines the 10−r left over, one for one.
y-m-38-06.s.s3.hint.1: Make a few tables that compare C(10,r) for r and 10−r.
y-m-38-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: With 10 kinds, I think it will be largest at r=... because ...
y-m-38-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I write both the place where it is largest and the reason?
y-m-38-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I explain that the values are symmetric left and right using the pairing of "choosing" and "leaving"?
y-m-38-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I compare the two equal values appearing side by side for 9 kinds with the case of 10 kinds?
y-m-38-06.s.s3.model.0: I think it will be largest at r=5. Choosing r kinds from 10 is the same as leaving 10−r kinds, so the values at r=4 and r=6 are equal, and for the middle one, 5, its pair is itself, so two equal values do not appear side by side. C(10,5)=252 is the largest.
y-m-38-06.s.s3.model.1: With 9 kinds the middle is 4.5, so 4 and 5 were equal at 126. With 10 kinds the middle is 5, so choosing 5 gives the most, and 4 and 6 are a pair, so they have the same value. The r chosen and the 10−r left are a pair, so the values are symmetric left and right.

y-m-38-07.title: A road with one section blocked by construction: how many ways are there to go around?
y-m-38-07.topic: Reflecting a blocked section in the shortest routes on a grid-shaped road
y-m-38-07.goal: Find and fix the error in a solution that subtracts the routes through the blocked section from the shortest routes on a grid road, compare the cases where the number of routes is the same depending on the position of the blocked section, and check with two methods.
y-m-38-07.material: There is a road shaped like a checkerboard, 4 squares wide and 3 squares tall. Intersections are written as (horizontal position, vertical position). The lower left (0,0) is A and the upper right (4,3) is B. You move only one square at a time, to the right (→) or up (↑). Because of construction, one horizontal road section joining (2,1) and (3,1) is blocked. Jimin worked out the number of ways to go from A to B without passing through the blocked section as follows.
y-m-38-07.thinking.0: Find the error in a solution
y-m-38-07.thinking.1: Compare results depending on the position of the section
y-m-38-07.thinking.2: Check the same value with different methods
y-m-38-07.prereq.0: H1 of this set is only a production difficulty level; it does not mean the Ministry of Education assigned it to a particular grade. Assume the basic counting unit (counting by splitting into cases, counting choices made one after another, the symbols nPr and nCr for permutations and combinations) has already been learned. You have counted the number of shortest routes going a squares right and b squares up by lining up the order.
y-m-38-07.s.s1.prompt: Pick the wrong line in Jimin's solution.
y-m-38-07.s.s1.hint.0: Choose one route from A to (2,1) and one route from (3,1) to B, and draw one route through the blocked section from start to finish.
y-m-38-07.s.s1.hint.1: List the routes you make that way and count how the 3 front parts and the 3 back parts pair up.
y-m-38-07.s.s1.line.0: If nothing were blocked, it would be the order of lining up → 4 times and ↑ 3 times, so choosing 3 places for ↑ among 7 steps gives C(7,3)=35 ways.
y-m-38-07.s.s1.line.1: From A to (2,1), line up → 2 times and ↑ 1 time, which is 3 ways.
y-m-38-07.s.s1.line.2: From (3,1) to B, line up → 1 time and ↑ 2 times, which is 3 ways.
y-m-38-07.s.s1.line.3: The routes through the blocked section are 3+3=6 ways.
y-m-38-07.s.s1.line.4: Therefore the number of ways to avoid the blocked section is 35−6=29.
y-m-38-07.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is wrong. A route through the blocked section is choosing "one of the 3 ways from A to (2,1)" and then choosing, in sequence, "one of the 3 ways from (3,1) to B." For each of the front 3 ways, the back 3 ways follow, so it is 3×3=9 ways. So it is 35−9=26 ways. Lines 1 to 3 are correct, and line 5 used the wrong 6.
y-m-38-07.s.s2.prompt: When the blocked section is one of the following sections instead of (2,1)–(3,1), choose all those where the number of ways to avoid the blocked section equals that of the first blocked case (26 ways).
y-m-38-07.s.s2.hint.0: For each option, write the two endpoints of the section, and find the number of routes through that section by splitting into (from A to the front endpoint) and (from the back endpoint to B).
y-m-38-07.s.s2.hint.1: Compare with the 9 you found for the original blocked section, and find the sections that give the same value.
y-m-38-07.s.s2.r.a: For routes through this section, 2 ways from A to (1,1) are followed by 6 ways from (2,1) to B, giving 12 ways. Then 35−12=23 ways remain, which differs from 26.
y-m-38-07.s.s2.r.b: This section is the original blocked section moved to the opposite side, about the center of the whole road. The routes through it are the same, 9 ways.
y-m-38-07.s.s2.r.c: For routes through this section, 4 ways from A to (3,1) are followed by 1 way from (4,1) to B, giving 4 ways. Then 35−4=31 ways remain, which differs from 26.
y-m-38-07.s.s2.r.d: The routes through this section are also 3 ways from A to (2,1) joined with 3 ways from (2,2) to B, which is 9, so 35−9=26 ways.
y-m-38-07.s.s2.r.e: The routes through the first horizontal section leaving A are 20 ways from (1,0) to B. Then 35−20=15 ways remain, which differs from 26.
y-m-38-07.s.s2.explain: Multiplying the number of shortest routes from A to the section's endpoint and from the other endpoint to B gives the number of routes through that section. Both b and d pass through 3×3=9 ways, so 35−9=26 ways. a is 12 ways (23 ways remain), c is 4 ways (31 ways remain), and e is 20 ways (15 ways remain). Even if the position of the blocked section differs, the value can be the same, and whether the section is horizontal or vertical does not matter.
y-m-38-07.s.s3.prompt: Explain with one of two methods that there are 26 ways to avoid the blocked section. ① Fix Jimin's solution correctly. ② Write in order, at each intersection, the number of ways to get there from A. (You cannot arrive by the blocked section.)
y-m-38-07.s.s3.hint.0: If you pick the first method, draw one route through the blocked section from start to finish, and write out, split up, how many such routes there are in all.
y-m-38-07.s.s3.hint.1: If you pick the second method, start from (0,0) and write the numbers for the intersections one row at a time, and at an intersection with a blocked section, first check from which side you can arrive.
y-m-38-07.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The routes through the blocked section are ... so ... ways.
y-m-38-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did I clearly write how I counted the routes through the blocked section (or how I handled the intersections)?
y-m-38-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I show with numbers what is subtracted from 35 and how much, or how the numbers at the intersections follow on?
y-m-38-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I check whether it also comes out to 26 with another method?
y-m-38-07.s.s3.model.0: For the routes through the blocked section, each of the 3 ways to get to (2,1) is followed by the 3 ways from (3,1) to B, so it is 3×3=9 ways. Subtracting these 9 from the 35 ways when nothing is blocked gives 26 ways.
y-m-38-07.s.s3.model.1: I wrote in order the number of ways to get from A to each intersection. You cannot arrive by the blocked section, so (3,1) is reached only from below and is 1 way, (4,1) is 2 ways, (3,2) is 7 ways, (4,2) is 9 ways, and (3,3) is 17 ways. Finally B is 17+9=26 ways.
